newsitem.title: CHILE: Spanish trial may ground Pinochet in Chile - lawyer.
newsitem.headline: Spanish trial may ground Pinochet in Chile - lawyer.

text.p: A trial in Spain against former Chilean military ruler Gen. Augusto Pinochet may never lead to his imprisonment but could cost the ex-dictator his freedom to travel to some places outside Chile, a prominent human rights lawyer said on Friday.
International arrest orders for Pinochet could prevent him from leaving Chile, at least to some parts of the world, if the trial ends in Pinochet's conviction in absentia, said lawyer Nelson Caucoto.

The Spanish high court, under Judge Manuel Garcia Castellon, is investigating the role of Chilean security forces in the deaths of at least 10 Spanish citizens on Chilean soil during Pinochet's rule from 1973 to 1990.
"I don't think he'll ever be able to travel freely through Europe again. He won't be able to go to Spain, Portugal or any country near the Iberian peninsula," said Caucoto.

Conviction could lead to an international Interpol warrant, which would make it difficult for him to travel in the Americas, said Caucoto, a well-known lawyer in human rights cases, in a meeting with the Chilean Foreign Press Association.

About 3,000 people were killed or "disappeared" at the hands of security forces during Pinochet's rule, according to a blue-ribbon commission formed after he yielded the presidency to an elected civilian in 1990. Pinochet is still commander-in-chief of the army and a powerful behind-the-scenes player in Chilean politics.

The current government of President Eduardo Frei has said it will not cooperate with the trial because Chile does not recognise the authority of other countries' courts to try crimes committed on its soil.
Pinochet, 81, makes only occasional trips abroad, visiting Britain in 1995 on the invitation of a munitions factory and later flying to Malaysia and last year Brazil.

A 1978 amnesty made it impossible to prosecute most atrocities committed under Pinochet's rule locally, leading rights groups to pursue some cases in foreign courts. But convictions in such cases have mostly symbolic value.
The Spanish trial's standing won a major boost last month when the United States said it would cooperate with the investigation, on instructions from Attorney General Janet Reno.
